Given only GIOS-SAMAR and Article VIII, Section 5(1), outline an objective answer to whether a fact-intensive petition should be filed directly in the Supreme Court.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Quiz • State action requirement

A private freight employee opens a package under the company's routine inspection policy, discovers illegal drugs, and then turns them over to police who had no prior involvement; was there a constitutional search?

Answer: No. A purely private search without government instigation or participation is not governed by Article III, Section 2.

Legal Basis: Article III, Sections 2 and 3(2) restrain unreasonable governmental searches and exclude evidence obtained in violation. People of the Philippines v. Andre Marti, G.R. No. 81561, January 18, 1991, teaches that The constitutional search-and-seizure guarantee restrains government, not a purely private search undertaken without police participation.

Application: The employee acted for the carrier and completed the inspection before police involvement; the officers merely received what the private actor found.

Conclusion: The drugs are not excluded on constitutional search-and-seizure grounds.

Article III, Sections 2 and 3(2) restrain unreasonable governmental searches and exclude evidence obtained in violation. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Andre Marti, G.R. No. 81561, January 18, 1991.
State action is ordinarily necessary for the constitutional exclusionary rule, although private conduct may be regulated by statute or civil law.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Quiz • Private search transformed into state action

Police ask a private courier to open every package sent by a named suspect and stand beside the employee while directing what compartments to inspect; may the State rely on the private-search doctrine?

Answer: No. A nominally private person becomes a government instrument when officers instigate, direct, or substantially participate in the search.

Legal Basis: Article III, Sections 2 and 3(2) require reasonableness and exclude fruits of an unconstitutional governmental search. People of the Philippines v. Andre Marti, G.R. Application: Here the targeted inspection was designed and supervised by police, so it is attributable to the State and must rest on a warrant or exception.

Conclusion: Absent a valid exception, the search and its fruits are inadmissible.

Article III, Sections 2 and 3(2) require reasonableness and exclude fruits of an unconstitutional governmental search. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Andre Marti, G.R. No. 81561, January 18, 1991.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Quiz • Substantive due process and police power
A regulation confiscates every lawfully transported farm animal and immediately gives it to a private charity without hearing, even when no disease or public danger is shown; is it valid?

Answer: No. The means are arbitrary and unduly oppressive in relation to the asserted regulatory purpose.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 1 protects property through substantive and procedural due process. Restituto Ynot v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 74457, March 20, 1987, teaches that Substantive due process requires a reasonable relation between lawful means and a legitimate end and forbids arbitrary confiscation.

Application: Automatic confiscation and donation without danger, standards, or hearing impose a drastic deprivation unrelated to demonstrated harm.

Conclusion: The regulation violates due process.
Article III, Section 1 protects property through substantive and procedural due process. Case authority: Restituto Ynot v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. 74457, March 20, 1987.
Police power requires a lawful public purpose and means reasonably necessary, not oppressive, and related to that purpose.

A law makes the apprehending officer the final judge of whether seized goods are forfeited, with no hearing or review; identify the due-process defect.

A city bans all short-time hotel admissions to discourage prostitution, including stays by travelers, families, and persons needing emergency shelter; does the ban satisfy substantive due process?

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 1 protects liberty and property against arbitrary police-power measures. White Light Corporation v. City of Manila, G.R. Application: The ordinance reaches every short stay without evidence of illegality and ignores less restrictive enforcement tools.

Conclusion: The blanket ban violates substantive due process.

When may a party challenge a police-power ordinance as facially invalid even though some applications might be lawful?

Answer: Facial invalidation outside the usual free-speech setting is exceptional, but may be warranted when the measure directly and broadly burdens fundamental liberty and lacks constitutionally valid applications under the controlling analysis.

Application: An ordinance categorically controlling intimate adult choices in every covered establishment presents broader liberty concerns than an ordinary economic rule.

Conclusion: The challenger must demonstrate the exceptional basis rather than invoke overbreadth mechanically.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Quiz • Cardinal primary rights
Enumerate and discuss the minimum administrative due-process requirement most directly violated when an agency decides a case using a secret report never disclosed to either party.

Answer: The core violation is the right to know and meet the evidence considered, together with the requirement that the decision rest on evidence in the record disclosed to the parties.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 1 applies due process to administrative adjudication; the cardinal primary rights operationalize it. Ang Tibay v. Court of Industrial Relations, G.R. No. L-46496, February 27, 1940, teaches that Administrative due process requires the cardinal primary rights, including a hearing, consideration of evidence, and a decision supported by substantial evidence disclosed to the parties.

Application: A secret report that supplies the outcome prevents testing accuracy and makes the hearing illusory.

Conclusion: The decision should be set aside or reopened for disclosure and response.

Article III, Section 1 applies due process to administrative adjudication; the cardinal primary rights operationalize it. Case authority: Ang Tibay v. Court of Industrial Relations, G.R. No. L-46496, February 27, 1940.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Quiz • Equal-protection classification
State the four requisites of a valid statutory classification under equal protection.

Answer: The classification must rest on substantial distinctions, be germane to the law's purpose, not be limited to existing conditions only, and apply equally to all members of the class.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 1 guarantees equal protection. Louis Biraogo v. Philippine Truth Commission of 2010, G.R. Application: A scholarship law for all indigent students based on financial need may satisfy the test; one naming only political supporters would not.

Conclusion: A classification failing any requisite is unconstitutional.

Answer: No. An official threat of future punishment that suppresses publication is a form of prior restraint carrying a heavy presumption of invalidity.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 4 protects speech, expression, and the press. Francisco I. Chavez v. Raul M. Gonzales, G.R. No. 168338, February 15, 2008, teaches that Government threats against media over future publication can be unconstitutional prior restraint and produce a chilling effect.

Application: The license threat comes before adjudication and predictably chills all broadcasters from airing the material.

Conclusion: The warning is unconstitutional.
Article III, Section 4 protects speech, expression, and the press. Case authority: Francisco I. Chavez v. Raul M. Gonzales, G.R. No. 168338, February 15, 2008.
Prior restraint is tolerated only in exceptional, narrowly defined circumstances supported by a compelling justification and proper legal process.

A court employee shows that a disciplinary rule substantially burdens a sincere religious practice; what must the State establish to deny an exemption?

Answer: The State must identify a compelling interest and prove that applying the rule to this claimant is the least restrictive means of achieving it.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 5 protects free exercise; the Constitution also bars establishment. Estrada v. Escritor, A.M. Does granting a narrowly tailored religious exemption necessarily violate the non-establishment clause?

Conclusion: The accommodation is constitutional if neutral, justified, and noncoercive.

Enumerate the elements used to determine when government occupation becomes a compensable taking.

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Date of taking and valuation
Government leased land for years under a voluntary contract and later filed expropriation after the owner rejected renewal; should valuation automatically use the first lease date?

Answer: No. A consensual lease does not ordinarily constitute taking; valuation is tied to the date the compulsory taking begins under law or the expropriation filing, as governing rules provide.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 9 requires payment of the full and fair equivalent at the legally determined time of taking. Republic of the Philippines v. Vda. de Castellvi, G.R. No. L-20620, August 15, 1974, teaches that Compensable taking requires entry under legal authority, more than momentary occupation, public use, deprivation of beneficial enjoyment, and an occupation not based on the owner's consent.

Application: Because initial entry rested on a lease, the later assertion of eminent domain marks the relevant taking absent proof that coercive deprivation began earlier.

Conclusion: Just compensation should be valued at the lawful date of compulsory taking.

Article III, Section 9 requires payment of the full and fair equivalent at the legally determined time of taking. Case authority: Republic of the Philippines v. Vda. de Castellvi, G.R. No. L-20620, August 15, 1974.
Consent and rental preserve the owner's contractual control and distinguish earlier occupancy from coercive appropriation.

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Complete custodial warnings
Before custodial questioning, is it enough for police to tell a suspect only, 'You may remain silent'?

Answer: No. The suspect must also be informed in an understandable manner of the right to competent and independent counsel, preferably of choice, that counsel will be provided if unaffordable, and the consequences and availability of those rights.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 12 and R.A. No. 7438 govern custodial rights and waiver. People of the Philippines v. Mahinay, G.R. No. 122485, February 1, 1999, teaches that Custodial rights include clear warnings, competent and independent counsel, and a written waiver made in counsel's presence.

Application: The single sentence omits counsel and waiver safeguards, so an ensuing uncounseled confession is constitutionally defective.

Conclusion: The confession is inadmissible unless independently shown to comply fully with the governing rights.
Article III, Section 12 and R.A. No. 7438 govern custodial rights and waiver. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Mahinay, G.R. No. 122485, February 1, 1999.
Warnings must be meaningful rather than ritual, and waiver must be in writing and made in counsel's presence.

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Waiver of custodial rights
A detained suspect signs a police-prepared waiver while alone after saying counsel would slow the investigation; is the waiver valid?

Answer: No. A waiver of custodial rights must be voluntary, knowing, intelligent, in writing, and made in the presence of counsel.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 12(1) and R.A. No. 7438 impose formal and substantive waiver requirements. People of the Philippines v. Mahinay, G.R. No. 122485, February 1, 1999, teaches that Custodial rights include clear warnings, competent and independent counsel, and a written waiver made in counsel's presence.

Application: Although written, the document was executed while the suspect was alone and therefore fails an express constitutional condition.

Conclusion: The waiver and confession are inadmissible.
Article III, Section 12(1) and R.A. No. 7438 impose formal and substantive waiver requirements. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Mahinay, G.R. No. 122485, February 1, 1999.
Police convenience or the suspect's unsupported impatience cannot replace counsel's protective presence.

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Media interview and custodial investigation
While in police custody, a suspect voluntarily asks to speak with an independent reporter and confesses on camera without police questioning; is Article III, Section 12 automatically violated?

Answer: No. The right governs custodial interrogation by law-enforcement agents or their instruments; a genuinely independent, spontaneous media interview is not automatically state interrogation.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 12 and R.A. No. 7438 protect persons under custodial investigation. People of the Philippines v. Felipe Andan y Hernández, G.R. No. 116437, March 3, 1997, teaches that A spontaneous statement to a private media interviewer is not custodial interrogation by police, although coercion or police orchestration would change the result.

Application: If the suspect initiated the interview and police neither directed questions nor pressured the statement, the confession is not excluded on that ground.

Conclusion: It may be admitted if voluntary and otherwise competent.
Article III, Section 12 and R.A. No. 7438 protect persons under custodial investigation. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Felipe Andan y Hernández, G.R. No. 116437, March 3, 1997.
The court must examine police orchestration, coercion, setting, and voluntariness; a reporter cannot be used as a constitutional workaround.

Police secretly give a reporter a list of questions and promise exclusive access if the reporter elicits a confession from a detained suspect; are custodial safeguards required?

Answer: Yes. The reporter functions as a police instrument, so the questioning is attributable to law enforcement.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 12 and R.A. No. 7438 cannot be evaded through a private intermediary. People of the Philippines v. Felipe Andan y Hernández, G.R. Application: The officers designed the interrogation and exchanged access for elicitation of admissions.

Conclusion: Absent valid warnings, counsel, and waiver, the confession is inadmissible.
Article III, Section 12 and R.A. No. 7438 cannot be evaded through a private intermediary. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Felipe Andan y Hernández, G.R. No. 116437, March 3, 1997.
Agency turns on government instigation and purpose, not the interviewer's professional label.

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Bail as right and discretion
Distinguish bail as a matter of right from bail as a matter of discretion before conviction.

Answer: Before conviction, bail is a right for offenses not punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment; for an offense carrying any of those penalties, bail is not a matter of right and must be denied when evidence of guilt is strong after hearing.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 13 and Rule 114 govern bail. Juan Ponce Enrile v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 213847, August 18, 2015, teaches that Bail is a matter of right before conviction except when the charged offense is punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment and evidence of guilt is strong; humanitarian circumstances may inform judicial discretion where bail is not a matter of right.

Application: A person charged with an offense carrying six years may demand reasonable bail, while one charged with plunder requires a hearing on strength of evidence.

Conclusion: Courts must apply the correct category and make supported findings.
Article III, Section 13 and Rule 114 govern bail. Case authority: Juan Ponce Enrile v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 213847, August 18, 2015.
The penalty prescribed by law, procedural stage, and strength of evidence determine the category; excessive bail remains forbidden.
Juan Ponce Enrile v. Sandiganbayan
G.R. No. 213847, August 18, 2015; ponente: Bersamin, J.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Humanitarian factors in discretionary bail
May advanced age and a life-threatening medical condition be considered when the court fixes or grants discretionary bail in a noncapital case punishable by reclusion perpetua?

Answer: Yes, as part of a reasoned discretionary assessment consistent with the presumption of innocence, flight risk, ability to stand trial, and the constitutional prohibition on excessive bail; they do not create an automatic entitlement.

Legal Basis: Article III, Sections 13 and 14 and Rule 114 guide discretionary bail. Juan Ponce Enrile v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 213847, August 18, 2015, teaches that Bail is a matter of right before conviction except when the charged offense is punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment and evidence of guilt is strong; humanitarian circumstances may inform judicial discretion where bail is not a matter of right.

Application: Verified severe illness, stable residence, and low flight risk may support stringent conditional release after hearing.

Conclusion: The court may grant reasonable conditional bail on a complete record.
Article III, Sections 13 and 14 and Rule 114 guide discretionary bail. Case authority: Juan Ponce Enrile v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 213847, August 18, 2015.
Humanitarian circumstances may bear on necessity and conditions, but the court must still address statutory penalty and evidence of guilt.

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Speedy disposition starting point
For constitutional speedy disposition, does the clock always begin with a confidential fact-finding audit conducted before any respondent is identified?

Answer: No. The period generally begins when formal investigation starts and the respondent is required to answer; preliminary fact-finding is ordinarily excluded unless used oppressively to evade the right.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 16 protects speedy disposition in judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative proceedings. Cesar Matas Cagang v. Sandiganbayan, Fifth Division, Office of the Ombudsman, and People of the Philippines, G.R. Nos. 206438, 206458 & 210141-42, July 31, 2018, teaches that Speedy-disposition analysis begins when formal investigation starts and balances length, reasons, assertion, and prejudice; fact-finding time is generally excluded.

Application: A routine confidential audit before charges and notice is normally not counted, but deliberate indefinite fact-finding after the case is ripe may be scrutinized.

Conclusion: The starting point depends on the proceeding's real formal and adversarial stage.

Article III, Section 16 protects speedy disposition in judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative proceedings. Case authority: Cesar Matas Cagang v. Sandiganbayan, Fifth Division, Office of the Ombudsman, and People of the Philippines, G.R. Nos. 206438, 206458 & 210141-42, July 31, 2018.
Courts balance length, reasons, assertion, and prejudice and determine when adversarial proceedings actually commenced.
Cesar Matas Cagang v. Sandiganbayan, Fifth Division, Office of the Ombudsman, and People of the Philippines

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Waiver and assertion of speedy disposition
An accused remains silent through years of justified defense continuances and invokes speedy disposition only after an adverse ruling; is dismissal automatic?

Answer: No. Assertion is one balancing factor, delay attributable to the defense is excluded, and the right is not measured by time alone.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 16 requires contextual balancing of length, cause, assertion, and prejudice. Cesar Matas Cagang v. Sandiganbayan, Fifth Division, Office of the Ombudsman, and People of the Philippines, G.R. Nos. 206438, 206458 & 210141-42, July 31, 2018, teaches that Speedy-disposition analysis begins when formal investigation starts and balances length, reasons, assertion, and prejudice; fact-finding time is generally excluded.

Application: Most delay here resulted from defense motions and no earlier demand or concrete prejudice is shown.

Conclusion: Dismissal is unwarranted on the stated facts.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Testimonial versus physical evidence
Does ordering an accused to provide handwriting exemplars violate the privilege against self-incrimination?

Answer: No. The privilege bars compelled testimonial communication, not compelled display or production of physical characteristics such as handwriting for comparison.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 17 protects against being compelled to be a witness against oneself. Francisco B. Chavez v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-29169, August 19, 1968, teaches that The privilege against self-incrimination protects testimonial compulsion, not the compelled production of a physical characteristic such as handwriting for comparison.

Application: Copying dictated neutral words reveals handwriting characteristics, not an admission to the offense.

Conclusion: The order does not violate the privilege, provided it is lawfully implemented.
Article III, Section 17 protects against being compelled to be a witness against oneself. Case authority: Francisco B. Chavez v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. L-29169, August 19, 1968.
The distinction turns on whether the accused is forced to disclose knowledge or merely furnish identifying physical evidence.

Investigators order a suspect to write from memory the secret password phrase used in the charged transaction; is this equivalent to an ordinary handwriting exemplar?

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Requisites of double jeopardy
Enumerate the requisites for former jeopardy to attach.

Answer: There must be a valid complaint or information, a court of competent jurisdiction, arraignment and valid plea, and acquittal, conviction, or dismissal without the accused's express consent after jeopardy attached.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 21 and Rule 117, Section 7 govern double jeopardy. People of the Philippines v. Aurelio Balisacan, G.R. No. L-26376, August 31, 1966, teaches that A guilty plea is vacated when the accused later asserts complete self-defense; an acquittal entered without a new plea and without allowing the prosecution to present evidence is void and does not create double jeopardy.

Application: If no valid plea was entered before a supposed acquittal, the accused was never lawfully put in jeopardy.

Conclusion: A later prosecution is barred only when all requisites concur and no recognized exception applies.
Article III, Section 21 and Rule 117, Section 7 govern double jeopardy. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Aurelio Balisacan, G.R. No. L-26376, August 31, 1966.
Each prerequisite protects finality of a valid prior exposure to criminal punishment; a void or premature proceeding does not suffice.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Improvident plea and jeopardy
A judge accepts an ambiguous 'I acted in self-defense' response as a guilty plea and immediately acquits without a valid arraignment; may the prosecution seek a proper trial?

Answer: Yes. A claim of self-defense is not an unconditional guilty plea, and an acquittal entered without valid arraignment and plea does not trigger jeopardy.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 21 and Rule 116 require a valid arraignment and plea; Rule 117 states the jeopardy requisites. People of the Philippines v. Aurelio Balisacan, G.R. No. L-26376, August 31, 1966, teaches that A guilty plea is vacated when the accused later asserts complete self-defense; an acquittal entered without a new plea and without allowing the prosecution to present evidence is void and does not create double jeopardy.

Application: The response admits the act but asserts justification, so the court should enter not guilty and try the case.

Conclusion: A proper prosecution is not barred.

Constitutional Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Ex post facto law
Define an ex post facto law and state whether the prohibition generally reaches purely civil regulation.

Answer: An ex post facto law retroactively: (1) criminalizes and punishes an act innocent when done; (2) aggravates a crime; (3) increases its punishment; (4) alters evidentiary rules to allow conviction on less or different proof; (5) disguises as civil regulation a penalty or deprivation for conduct lawful when done; or (6) removes a legal protection already available to the accused. A genuinely civil, nonpunitive measure ordinarily falls outside the prohibition.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 22 prohibits ex post facto laws and bills of attainder. In the Matter of the Petition for the Declaration of the Petitioner's Rights and Duties Under Section 8 of R.A. No. 6132; Kay Villegas Kami, Inc., G.R. No. L-32485, October 22, 1970, teaches that An ex post facto law retroactively criminalizes an innocent act, aggravates a crime, increases punishment, lowers the proof needed to convict, disguises a penalty as civil regulation, or removes a protection already available to the accused; the prohibition concerns penal or punitive operation.

Application: A retroactive increase in imprisonment for completed conduct is prohibited; a genuinely remedial filing procedure with no punitive effect ordinarily is not.

Conclusion: The prohibition applies when retroactivity imposes one of the recognized penal disadvantages.

Article III, Section 22 prohibits ex post facto laws and bills of attainder. Case authority: In the Matter of the Petition for the Declaration of the Petitioner's Rights and Duties Under Section 8 of R.A. No. 6132; Kay Villegas Kami, Inc., G.R. No. L-32485, October 22, 1970.
Courts examine retroactive operation and punitive effect, not legislative label alone.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD302 • Final • Bill of attainder
Congress enacts a statute naming five activists, declaring them members of an illegal organization, and imposing imprisonment without trial; what constitutional prohibition is violated?

Answer: The statute is a bill of attainder because it legislatively determines guilt and imposes punishment on identified persons without judicial trial.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 22 prohibits bills of attainder. People of the Philippines v. Hon. Simeon N. Ferrer, Feliciano Co, and Nilo S. Tayag, G.R. Nos. L-32613-14, December 27, 1972, teaches that A bill of attainder legislatively determines guilt and inflicts punishment without judicial trial; a law requiring the State to prove the accused's knowing, willful conduct and specific intent in court is not a bill of attainder.

Application: The law names the targets, adjudges membership, and directly orders imprisonment, leaving courts no genuine determination of guilt.

Conclusion: The statute is unconstitutional.
Article III, Section 22 prohibits bills of attainder. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Hon. Simeon N. Ferrer, Feliciano Co, and Nilo S. Tayag, G.R. Nos. L-32613-14, December 27, 1972.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Quiz • treason elements and overt act
Enumerate the elements of treason and explain the two-witness rule?

Answer: Treason requires allegiance to the Philippines, war in which the Philippines is involved, and either levying war against the Government or adhering to enemies by giving aid or comfort; conviction requires two witnesses to the same overt act or confession in open court.

Legal Basis: Articles 114 and 115 of the Revised Penal Code. The Revised Penal Code defines crimes against national security, public order, public officers, persons, liberty, honor, and property; its elements must be strictly proved and its monetary penalties are read with current amendments.

Application: Political sympathy alone is insufficient; the prosecution must prove an overt act of aid or comfort with the specially required quantum and form of evidence.

Conclusion: Both the substantive elements and special evidentiary safeguard must be satisfied.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Quiz • rebellion and absorption
Rebels kill soldiers and burn a military depot as overt acts to advance their uprising; may they be charged with rebellion complexed with murder and arson?

Answer: No. Under the Hernandez doctrine, common crimes committed in furtherance or on the occasion of rebellion are absorbed in simple rebellion rather than complexed under Article 48.

Legal Basis: Articles 134 and 135 of the Revised Penal Code. Under the controlling Hernandez doctrine, common crimes committed in furtherance of or on the occasion of rebellion are absorbed in simple rebellion and cannot be charged as rebellion complexed with murder.

Application: The killings and burning are alleged as means and overt acts of the political uprising, not private crimes wholly independent of it.

Conclusion: The proper charge is simple rebellion.

The Revised Penal Code defines crimes against national security, public order, public officers, persons, liberty, honor, and property; its elements must be strictly proved and its monetary penalties are read with current amendments.

Application: The cashier is accountable by office, received the collections, and offers no credible explanation for the shortage after demand.

Conclusion: The statutory inference supports malversation, subject to rebuttal and proof beyond reasonable doubt.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Midterm • fair comment and actual malice
A columnist expresses a harsh opinion about a public-interest conference based on disclosed, substantially true facts; is presumed malice alone enough for libel liability?

Answer: No. Fair comment on a matter of public interest is qualifiedly privileged; the privilege defeats presumed malice and requires proof that the speaker knew the factual assertion was false or recklessly disregarded its truth.

Legal Basis: Articles 353 and 354 of the Revised Penal Code and Article III, Section 4 of the Constitution. Fair comment on matters of public interest is qualifiedly privileged beyond Article 354's express examples; privilege removes presumed malice and requires proof of actual malice, while the offended person must also be identifiable to a third person.

Application: The opinion is tied to disclosed facts and public activity, so liability requires actual malice rather than the ordinary presumption.

Conclusion: Absent actual malice and adequate identifiability, libel liability does not attach.

One user authors a defamatory social-media post while another merely clicks a reaction button; may both be convicted of cyberlibel under Section 4(c)(4)?

Conclusion: Only the original author is potentially liable on these facts.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Midterm • bigamy and void marriages

An accused proves that the first marriage was void from the beginning for total absence of a marriage license, although no nullity judgment existed before the second marriage; is that a defense to bigamy?

Answer: Yes. Pulido holds that a void ab initio first or second marriage may be collaterally shown as a defense to bigamy even without a prior nullity decree; the rule differs for a merely voidable marriage.

Legal Basis: Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code and Articles 35, 40, and 41 of the Family Code. A void ab initio first or second marriage is a defense to bigamy even without a prior judicial declaration of nullity; a merely voidable marriage remains valid until annulled and does not provide the same defense.

Application: If the total absence of a license is competently proved and no exception applies, no valid subsisting first marriage existed as Article 349 requires.

Conclusion: The accused should be acquitted if the voidness is proved beyond the prosecution's case.

Criminal Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Midterm • concubinage
Enumerate the statutory modes by which a married man commits concubinage?

Answer: A married man commits concubinage by keeping a mistress in the conjugal dwelling, having sexual intercourse under scandalous circumstances with a woman not his wife, or cohabiting with her in another place; the woman must know he is married.

Legal Basis: Articles 334 and 344 of the Revised Penal Code. The Revised Penal Code defines crimes against national security, public order, public officers, persons, liberty, honor, and property; its elements must be strictly proved and its monetary penalties are read with current amendments.

Application: Proof of isolated clandestine intercourse without scandal, cohabitation, or keeping a mistress in the conjugal home does not by itself fit the statutory modes.

Conclusion: Liability depends on proof of one enumerated mode and a proper complaint.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Midterm • acts of lasciviousness
With lewd design, an adult forcibly touches another person's intimate parts but performs no act amounting to rape; what offense may arise?

Answer: Acts of lasciviousness may arise when the offender commits a lewd act under any circumstance in Article 266-A's first paragraph and the conduct does not constitute rape or another more specific offense.

Legal Basis: Article 336 in relation to Article 266-A of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by R.A. No. 11648. R.A. No. 11648 raised the statutory-rape threshold to under sixteen, created a narrowly defined close-in-age exception, and conformed related sexual-offense age provisions.

Application: The intentional intimate touching, force, and lewd purpose satisfy the offense if no penetration or other act completes rape and no special child statute controls.

Conclusion: The offender may be liable for acts of lasciviousness.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Midterm • statutory rape and close-in-age exception
A nineteen-year-old has purportedly consensual sexual intercourse with a fifteen-year-old who is not the older person's spouse; does R.A. No. 11648's close-in-age exception apply?

Answer: No. Carnal knowledge of a person under sixteen is statutory rape, and the close-in-age exception requires an age difference of not more than three years, a consensual, nonabusive, nonexploitative act, and a victim at least thirteen.

Legal Basis: Article 266-A(1)(d) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by R.A. No. 11648. R.A. No. 11648 raised the statutory-rape threshold to under sixteen, created a narrowly defined close-in-age exception, and conformed related sexual-offense age provisions.

Application: The four-year age difference exceeds the statutory limit, so purported consent does not remove liability.

Conclusion: Statutory rape is committed if carnal knowledge and ages are proved.

Criminal Law II
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Midterm • attempted versus consummated rape
An erect penis only grazes the mons pubis and never enters or touches either labium before the victim escapes; is rape consummated?

Answer: No. Consummation requires the erect penis to enter or touch either labium; mere epidermal grazing of the mons pubis or external surface does not cross that threshold, though attempted rape may exist if overt acts and intent are proved.

Legal Basis: Articles 6 and 266-A of the Revised Penal Code, as amended. Consummated penile rape requires entry into or touching of either labium by an erect penis; mere grazing of the mons pubis or external surface without that threshold is not consummation and may constitute attempted rape or another offense.

Application: The described contact remains outside both labia, while the attack and interruption may establish commencement of execution without voluntary desistance.

Conclusion: The proper stage is attempted rape, subject to proof of intent and overt acts.

A person with moral ascendancy induces a fourteen-year-old child to perform lascivious conduct in exchange for money; may R.A. No. 7610 apply even without penile penetration?

Application: The child's age, consideration, lascivious act, and offender's influence support sexual-abuse liability independent of penetration.

Conclusion: R.A. No. 7610 may apply, subject to precise pleading and avoidance of duplicative punishment.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Final • trafficking in children
A recruiter transports a seventeen-year-old to work in commercial sexual exploitation without proving force, fraud, or coercion; is trafficking possible?

Answer: Yes. When the trafficked person is a child, recruitment, transport, transfer, harboring, obtaining, maintaining, offering, or receiving for exploitation is trafficking even without proof of the prohibited means required for adult victims.

Legal Basis: Sections 3 and 4 of R.A. No. 9208, as amended by R.A. Nos. 10364 and 11862. The expanded law punishes recruitment, obtaining, transporting, maintaining, offering, or receiving persons by prohibited means for exploitation; prohibited means need not be shown when the trafficked person is a child.

Application: The victim is under eighteen and was moved for commercial sexual exploitation, satisfying the act-and-purpose framework.

Conclusion: Trafficking in persons may be established without proof of force or fraud.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Final • illegal sale of dangerous drugs
What are the essential transaction facts the prosecution must prove for illegal sale of dangerous drugs?

Answer: The prosecution must prove the identities of buyer and seller, the object and consideration, and delivery of the drug and payment, while establishing that the presented drug is the same seized item through an unbroken, legally adequate chain of custody.

Legal Basis: Sections 5 and 21 of R.A. No. 9165, as amended by R.A. No. 10640. R.A. No. 9165 defines illegal sale and possession of dangerous drugs and Section 21, as amended, prescribes inventory, witness, and preservation safeguards for seized items.

Application: A poseur-buyer's testimony about offer, delivery, and payment is not enough if the corpus delicti's identity and integrity are left doubtful.

Conclusion: Both sale and preservation of the seized drug must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Final • drug chain of custody
Officers omit the required inventory witnesses and give no justification in their affidavits, while one custody transfer is undocumented; may regular performance cure the gaps?

Answer: No. Noncompliance may be excused only on proved justifiable grounds with preservation of integrity and evidentiary value; unexplained witness and custody gaps cannot be replaced by the presumption of regularity.

Legal Basis: Section 21 of R.A. No. 9165, as amended by R.A. No. 10640. The prosecution must establish every material link in drug custody and explain noncompliance with Section 21 in sworn statements while showing preservation of integrity and evidentiary value; unexplained lapses create reasonable doubt.

Application: The affidavits identify no concrete impediment and the missing transfer leaves the fungible item vulnerable to substitution or contamination.

Conclusion: Reasonable doubt requires acquittal.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Final • entrapment and instigation
Distinguish entrapment from instigation when an undercover officer participates in a prohibited sale?

Answer: Entrapment merely provides an opportunity and catches a person pursuing an independently formed criminal design, and is lawful; instigation originates the criminal idea in government and induces an otherwise unwilling person to commit it, and is an absolutory cause.

Legal Basis: The Revised Penal Code's requirement of criminal intent and controlling entrapment jurisprudence. Philippine law distinguishes lawful entrapment, which merely catches an offender pursuing an existing criminal design, from instigation, in which government originates and induces the crime and which is an absolutory cause.

Application: If the suspect already offered to sell and the officer only posed as buyer, it is entrapment; if persistent official pressure created the plan in an innocent person, it is instigation.

Conclusion: Liability turns on the origin of the criminal design and police conduct.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Final • carnapping with homicide
A person takes another's motor vehicle by force with intent to gain and kills the driver during the taking; what offense is committed?

Answer: The offender commits carnapping in the aggravated form where the owner, driver, or occupant is killed in the course of carnapping, punishable under R.A. No. 10883.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD402 • Final • proximate cause in homicide
A victim's minor wound fully heals, but months later the victim dies from an unrelated disease; may the assailant be convicted of homicide based only on temporal sequence?

Answer: No. The prosecution must prove that the assault was the proximate cause of death—an unbroken natural and logical cause without an efficient intervening cause.

Legal Basis: Article 4 in relation to Article 249 of the Revised Penal Code. Criminal liability for a resulting death requires proof beyond reasonable doubt that the accused's act was the proximate cause—an unbroken, natural and logical cause without an efficient intervening event.

Application: Complete healing and an independently fatal disease break the causal chain absent medical proof connecting the wound to death.

Conclusion: Homicide is not proved beyond reasonable doubt, although liability for the original injury may remain.

Define a civil obligation and identify its four essential elements.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Sources of obligations
Enumerate the five sources of obligations under the Civil Code and explain why the list matters.

Answer: Obligations arise from law, contracts, quasi-contracts, acts or omissions punished by law, and quasi-delicts.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1157 supplies the exclusive statutory classification, while Articles 1158 to 1162 state the governing rules for each source.

Application: A claimant cannot demand payment merely because it seems fair; the claim must be linked to one recognized source and its requisites.

Conclusion: Identify the source first because it determines the elements, defenses, and governing rules.
Civil Code Article 1157 supplies the exclusive statutory classification, while Articles 1158 to 1162 state the governing rules for each source.
Civil obligations must be traced to a source recognized by Article 1157.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Obligations arising from law
May a court presume an obligation allegedly created by statute when the statute does not expressly impose it?

Answer: No; obligations arising from law are not presumed and are demandable only when expressly determined by the Civil Code or a special law.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1158 requires an express legal basis and regulates the obligation first by the creating law, then suppletorily by Book IV.

Application: A party who points only to a broad policy declaration but no provision creating the claimed payment duty has not established a legal obligation.

Conclusion: The alleged statutory duty is unenforceable absent an express legal foundation.
Civil Code Article 1158 requires an express legal basis and regulates the obligation first by the creating law, then suppletorily by Book IV.
Legal obligations are exceptional and cannot be created by implication alone.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Contracts as law between the parties
A buyer later finds a freely accepted payment schedule inconvenient; may the buyer disregard it solely for that reason?

Answer: No, absent a valid ground for modification, avoidance, or relief, the buyer remains bound by the lawful stipulation.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1159 gives contractual obligations the force of law and requires good-faith compliance; Articles 1306 and 1315 reinforce contractual autonomy and binding effect from perfection.

Application: Mere inconvenience does not invalidate the schedule, although an illegal, unconscionable, or otherwise defective term may be challenged under the Code.

Conclusion: The buyer must comply or establish a recognized legal ground for relief.
Civil Code Article 1159 gives contractual obligations the force of law and requires good-faith compliance; Articles 1306 and 1315 reinforce contractual autonomy and binding effect from perfection.
A valid contract binds the parties as law and must be performed in good faith.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Good faith in performance
Explain the role of good faith in the performance of a contract even when every operational detail is not written.

Answer: Good faith requires each party to perform express promises and the consequences that, according to the contract’s nature, usage, and law, are necessary to give the agreement honest effect.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1159 and 1315 bind parties to good-faith performance and to consequences consistent with the contract’s nature, usage, and law.

Application: A financing institution may not exploit an omitted ministerial step to frustrate the central housing arrangement while insisting on literal performance from the other side.

Conclusion: Good faith supplies faithful implementation, not authority to rewrite the bargain.

Contractual good faith is part of performance but cannot contradict clear lawful terms.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Obligation to give a determinate thing
What duties accompany an obligation to deliver a determinate thing before actual delivery?

Answer: The debtor must preserve the thing with the required diligence, deliver its accessions and accessories, and answer for loss or deterioration attributable to fault, delay, or an assumed risk.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1163, 1164, 1166, and 1173 govern preservation, fruits, accessions, accessories, and diligence.

Application: A seller of a specifically identified machine must reasonably safeguard it and deliver its included components rather than leave it exposed to avoidable damage.

Conclusion: The duty to deliver includes interim preservation and the legally included components.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Obligations to do and not to do
Distinguish the creditor’s remedies when an obligation to do is not performed and when an obligation not to do is violated.

Answer: For nonperformance or defective performance of an obligation to do, proper performance may be executed at the debtor’s cost and poorly done work may be undone; for violation of an obligation not to do, the forbidden act may be undone at the debtor’s expense, with damages when proper.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1167, 1168, and 1170 govern substituted performance, undoing, and damages.

Application: A contractor who installs the wrong material may bear correction costs, while a tenant who builds despite a no-build covenant may be compelled to remove the structure.

Conclusion: The remedy seeks conformity with the promised positive or negative prestation.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Mora solvendi and demand
A note is payable on June 1 but contains no automatic-default clause; when does the debtor ordinarily incur legal delay?

Answer: Ordinarily, the debtor incurs delay only from judicial or extrajudicial demand made after the obligation becomes due.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1169 makes demand the general trigger for delay, subject to its stated exceptions.

Application: The June 1 maturity makes the debt demandable, but without a contractual or statutory exception, damages for mora generally run from the creditor’s demand, not automatically from midnight on June 1.

Conclusion: Delay begins upon valid demand unless an Article 1169 exception applies.

Maturity and legal delay are distinct; demand is ordinarily required for mora solvendi.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Exceptions to demand
Enumerate the instances when demand is unnecessary to place an obligor in delay.

Answer: Demand is unnecessary when the obligation or law expressly so declares, time was a controlling motive, demand would be useless because performance was made impossible, or—within reciprocal obligations—one party has performed and the other fails to perform.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1169 states the exceptions and the special rule for reciprocal obligations.

Application: A caterer engaged specifically for a wedding date is in delay upon failure to appear because performance after the event defeats the controlling purpose.

Conclusion: An exception must be tied to the law, stipulation, purpose, impossibility, or reciprocal performance.
Civil Code Article 1169 states the exceptions and the special rule for reciprocal obligations.
Demand may be dispensed with only on an Article 1169 ground.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Quiz • Fortuitous event
State the requisites of a fortuitous-event defense and apply them to a contractor who was already in delay before war closed the project site.

Answer: The defense generally requires an independent, unforeseeable or unavoidable event that made performance impossible despite due care and without debtor participation; a debtor already in delay ordinarily remains liable.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1174 and 1165 qualify exemption for fortuitous events, while the obligation, stipulation, or nature of the undertaking may allocate the risk.

Application: Even if the closure was beyond control, the contractor cannot rely on it to erase liability for performance that should already have been completed before the closure.

Conclusion: The prior delay defeats complete exemption for the resulting loss.

Fortuitous event excuses only a debtor free from fault, delay, and assumed risk, and only when the event truly prevents performance.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Midterm • Pure, conditional, and period obligations
Distinguish a pure obligation, a conditional obligation, and an obligation with a period.

Answer: A pure obligation is immediately demandable; a conditional obligation depends on an uncertain future event or an unknown past event; an obligation with a period depends on a future event certain to arrive.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1179, 1181, and 1193 provide the classifications and their demandability.

Application: “Pay now” is pure, “pay if the permit is granted” is conditional, and “pay on December 1” carries a period.

Conclusion: Classify by whether the qualifying event is absent, uncertain, or certain.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Midterm • Potestative conditions
D promises to pay C ₱500,000 “if I alone later decide that I want to be bound”; is the obligation valid?

Answer: No; a suspensive condition that makes the birth of the obligation depend solely on the debtor’s will voids the conditional obligation.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1182 voids a condition dependent solely on the debtor’s will, while chance or third-person conditions may take effect.

Application: D’s clause leaves both the existence and enforceability of the promise entirely to D, so no effective juridical necessity arises.

Conclusion: The obligation is void as purely potestative at inception.
Civil Code Article 1182 voids a condition dependent solely on the debtor’s will, while chance or third-person conditions may take effect.
A purely potestative suspensive condition on the birth of an obligation is void.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Midterm • Mixed conditions
A buyer will pay the balance once the seller obtains a right of way from independent neighboring owners; is the condition void as potestative?

Answer: No; the condition is mixed because fulfillment depends not only on a party’s will but also on independent third persons.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1182 recognizes conditions dependent on chance or a third person; Catungal treated negotiation with neighboring owners as a valid mixed condition.

Application: The seller can exert effort but cannot compel the neighbors to grant the easement, so fulfillment is not under one debtor’s exclusive control.

Conclusion: The mixed condition is valid and governs demandability.

A developer promised a final payment once inspection occurred, then barred the inspector solely to avoid paying; is the condition fulfilled?

Answer: Yes, if the developer intentionally and actually prevented the suspensive condition, it is deemed constructively fulfilled.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1186 applies when the obligor voluntarily prevents fulfillment; the doctrine requires intent to prevent and actual prevention.

Application: The developer’s deliberate exclusion, rather than an external cause, made inspection impossible and cannot be used to defeat the payment duty.

Conclusion: The inspection condition is deemed fulfilled.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Midterm • Reciprocal obligations and substantial breach
May a party resolve a reciprocal contract for every slight or casual breach?

Answer: No; resolution under Article 1191 generally requires a substantial and fundamental breach that defeats the object of the parties, not a slight or casual violation.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1191 implies the power of resolution in reciprocal obligations; jurisprudence limits it to a breach of faith affecting reciprocity.

Application: A minor, promptly corrected reporting delay ordinarily does not justify undoing a fully performed transfer, unlike refusal to deliver the principal consideration.

Conclusion: Only a substantial breach supports resolution on these facts.

What remedies may the injured party elect under Article 1191 when the other party substantially breaches a reciprocal obligation?

Application: An unpaid seller may demand the price or seek resolution for a substantial failure to pay, but cannot obtain inconsistent double recovery.

After valid resolution of a reciprocal sale, may the seller retain both the goods and all payments without a lawful forfeiture basis?

Answer: Ordinarily no; resolution requires mutual restitution so each party returns what was received, subject to lawful damages and special rules.

Application: The buyer returns the delivered equipment and the seller returns the partial price; proven damages may then be addressed separately.

When may a court fix the period for performance under Article 1197?

Answer: A court may fix the period when no period is stated but the nature and circumstances show one was intended, or when the duration depends on the debtor’s will.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1197 directs the court to determine the period probably contemplated by the parties.

Application: A promise to build a public facility with no deadline may imply a reasonable period, though fixing a period becomes needless where an extraordinary lapse has already made the procedure futile.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Midterm • Alternative and facultative obligations
Distinguish an alternative obligation from a facultative obligation.

Answer: In an alternative obligation, several prestations are due but complete performance of one extinguishes the obligation; in a facultative obligation, only one prestation is due while another may be substituted.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1199 to 1206 govern alternative obligations and Article 1206 governs facultative substitution.

Application: “Deliver 100 reams or pay ₱50,000” is alternative; “deliver the named printer, with the option to substitute a scanner” is facultative.

A single package agreement grants a multiple-order discount for three machines serving one rollout; may the seller treat each unit as an independent divisible contract after delivering only one?

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1223 to 1225 make divisibility depend on the prestation, law, and especially party intent, not physical severability alone.

Application: One agreement, one package discount, and one integrated rollout support indivisibility even though each machine is physically separable.

To whom must payment be made to extinguish an obligation?

Answer: Payment must be made to the creditor, the creditor’s successor in interest, or a person authorized to receive it; payment to a third person is valid only to the extent it benefits the creditor, subject to statutory exceptions.

Application: A debtor who pays an unrelated collector without authority remains liable unless the creditor ratified the payment or actually received its benefit.

May a debtor compel a creditor to accept a different object or partial payment when the contract requires full delivery of a determinate prestation?

Define dacion en pago and state its essential requisites.

May legal compensation occur when one of two asserted debts is contingent and not yet liquidated?

Application: A contingent obligation whose amount depends on prior payment by a third party is neither presently due nor liquidated, so it cannot offset a final restitution debt.

State the general post-Nacar framework for interest on a monetary award when no valid written rate governs.

State the principle and limits of freedom of contract.

Answer: Parties may establish terms they deem convenient, but stipulations cannot be contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1306 defines contractual autonomy and its limits; Articles 1409 and 1416 address unlawful agreements and public-policy exceptions.

Application: A long lease designed as a virtual transfer of land to an alien cannot be saved by consent because it circumvents a constitutional prohibition.

Conclusion: Freedom of contract ends where mandatory law and public policy begin.
Civil Code Article 1306 defines contractual autonomy and its limits; Articles 1409 and 1416 address unlawful agreements and public-policy exceptions.
Contractual autonomy is broad but subordinate to mandatory norms.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Final • Mutuality of contracts
A supply contract lets only the buyer determine after delivery whether it will pay anything, using no objective standard; is the clause valid?

Answer: No; validity and compliance cannot be left to the will of one party alone, although performance may be entrusted to a third person or measured by an objective standard subject to the Code.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1308 to 1310 require mutuality and regulate third-person determination.

Application: The buyer’s unreviewable discretion destroys reciprocal binding force; a market-price formula or independent appraiser would be materially different.

Conclusion: The purely unilateral payment clause violates mutuality.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Final • Relativity of contracts
May a stranger ordinarily sue to enforce a contract to which the stranger is neither party, heir, nor assign?

Answer: No; contracts generally take effect only between the parties, their assigns, and heirs, subject to nontransmissibility and recognized exceptions such as a valid stipulation pour autrui.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 1311 states relativity and the third-party-beneficiary exception.

Application: A neighbor who gains only an incidental advantage from a lease has no enforcement right unless the contract deliberately and clearly confers a benefit accepted before revocation.

Conclusion: The stranger cannot enforce the contract on the stated facts.

What requisites permit a third person to demand performance of a stipulation pour autrui?

Answer: The contract must clearly and deliberately confer a benefit on the third person, the benefit must not be merely incidental, and the beneficiary must communicate acceptance to the obligor before revocation.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Final • Perfection and essential requisites
When is a consensual contract perfected, and what essential requisites must concur?

An offeree emails a qualified acceptance that changes the price; is a contract perfected?

Application: Changing the price rejects the original terms and proposes a new bargain that the original offeror must accept.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Final • Option contracts
An option to sell land lacks consideration separate from the purchase price; the offeree accepts before withdrawal. Is the seller bound?

Answer: Yes; without separate consideration the option is not an independently binding option contract, but it remains an offer that may be accepted before withdrawal, producing a reciprocal contract.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1324 and 1479, as reconciled by the controlling Sanchez doctrine reaffirmed in PNOC v. Keppel, govern.

Application: Because acceptance was communicated while the offer still subsisted, the absence of separate option money does not prevent perfection of the sale agreement.

Conclusion: The timely accepted offer binds the seller.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Final • Capacity and vices of consent
Differentiate incapacity to give consent from mistake, violence, intimidation, undue influence, and fraud.

Answer: Incapacity concerns a person whom law does not allow to give effective consent; the listed vices concern consent given by a legally capable person but formed without adequate intelligence, freedom, or spontaneity.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1327 to 1330 and 1390 classify incapable-party and vitiated-consent contracts as voidable, subject to applicable law.

Application: A capable adult deceived about a decisive fact may seek annulment for fraud, while a minor’s contract raises legal capacity rather than deception.

Conclusion: Identify whether the defect lies in legal capacity or in the quality of consent.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Final • Mistake
What kind of mistake vitiates consent under Article 1331?

Answer: The mistake must concern the substance of the object or principal conditions that chiefly moved a party to contract, or the identity or qualifications of a party when principally causal; a simple accounting error is corrected rather than annulling consent.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1331 to 1334 govern mistake and mutual error of legal effect.

Application: Mistaking a parcel’s zoning when that lawful use was the decisive premise may be substantial; misadding one installment is ordinarily correctable.

Conclusion: Only a material causal mistake makes the contract voidable.

Distinguish violence from intimidation as vices of consent and state the test for intimidation.

Answer: Violence uses serious or irresistible physical force; intimidation creates a reasonable and well-grounded fear of imminent and grave evil to person or property, assessed with the victim’s age, sex, and condition.

Distinguish dolo causante from dolo incidente and state the remedy for each.

Answer: Causal fraud is serious deception without which the party would not have contracted and may make the contract voidable; incidental fraud affects performance or secondary terms and ordinarily gives rise only to damages.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1338 and 1344 distinguish fraud inducing consent from incidental fraud.

Application: A bounced balance check issued after the seller had already decided to sell may constitute breach or incidental fraud rather than the decisive inducement to the sale.

Conclusion: Annulment requires proof that serious fraud caused the consent itself.

Distinguish absolute from relative simulation and state their effects.

Distinguish the object from the cause of a contract and state the requisites of each.

Does the Statute of Frauds make every oral sale of land void?

Answer: No; it generally makes a covered executory agreement unenforceable unless evidenced by the required writing, and it does not apply in the same way after total or partial performance; separate formalities may be required for validity or third-party effect.

Distinguish interpretation of a contract from reformation of an instrument.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD502 • Final • Defective contracts
Distinguish rescissible, voidable, unenforceable, and void or inexistent contracts by defect and remedy.

Answer: A rescissible contract is valid but causes legally specified damage and is subsidiarily rescinded; a voidable contract binds until annulled and may be ratified; an unenforceable contract cannot be sued upon unless ratified; a void contract has no legal effect and generally cannot be ratified.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1380 to 1422 establish the four classes, their grounds, prescription rules, ratification, and effects.

Conclusion: The remedy and effect follow the precise class of defect, not the loose label “invalid.”

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • liberal construction of procedural rules

A complaint was timely filed, but counsel omitted a nonprejudicial formal detail and corrected it immediately after notice; should the action automatically be dismissed in the name of strict compliance?

Answer: No. Procedural rules must be enforced, but a harmless formal lapse that is promptly cured may be relaxed when no substantive right is impaired and dismissal would defeat, rather than advance, a just, speedy, and inexpensive determination.

Legal Basis: Rule 1, Section 6 of the Rules of Court. Procedure serves justice; although timely full docket fees are ordinarily mandatory, a court may relax a directory dismissal rule in an exceptional meritorious case where the shortfall resulted from the court officer's assessment and was promptly cured.

Application: The omission caused no surprise or prejudice and was corrected at once, so proportional enforcement favors allowing the case to proceed while requiring full compliance.

Conclusion: The court should accept the correction and deny automatic dismissal.
Rule 1, Section 6 of the Rules of Court. G.R. No. 140162, November 22, 2000, Mendoza, J. — petition granted; dismissal of appeal reversed and case remanded
Procedural rules are liberally construed to promote a just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition, without excusing jurisdictional or prejudicial noncompliance.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • elements of a cause of action
Define a cause of action and illustrate its three elements using an unpaid matured loan?

Answer: A cause of action is the act or omission by which one party violates the right of another; its elements are a legal right in the plaintiff, a correlative obligation in the defendant, and an act or omission violating that right.

Legal Basis: Rule 2, Section 2 of the Rules of Court. A cause of action is the act or omission violating another's right; failure to state one is tested from the complaint's allegations, hypothetically admitted, together with controlling law of which the court may take notice.

Application: A lender has the right to payment, the borrower must pay at maturity, and the borrower's unjustified nonpayment after maturity breaches that duty.

Conclusion: Those allegations state a cause of action for collection.

A cause of action consists of the plaintiff's right, the defendant's correlative duty, and the defendant's violation of that right.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • failure to state versus lack of cause of action
Distinguish failure to state a cause of action from failure to prove the cause of action alleged?

Answer: Failure to state a cause of action is a pleading defect tested from the complaint's allegations and controlling law, while failure to prove the pleaded cause is an evidentiary deficiency ordinarily resolved after the plaintiff rests.

Legal Basis: Rule 2, Section 2; Rule 8, Section 12(a)(4); and Rule 33, Section 1 of the Rules of Court. A cause of action is the act or omission violating another's right; failure to state one is tested from the complaint's allegations, hypothetically admitted, together with controlling law of which the court may take notice.

Application: A complaint omitting the defendant's breach may be dismissed on an affirmative defense; a complete complaint unsupported at trial is vulnerable to demurrer to evidence.

Conclusion: The first attacks allegations; the second attacks proof.
Rule 2, Section 2; Rule 8, Section 12(a)(4); and Rule 33, Section 1 of the Rules of Court. G.R. No. 198680, July 8, 2013, Perlas-Bernabe, J. — petition denied; dismissal affirmed without prejudice

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • splitting a single cause of action
A lender separately sues for the principal and then for interest arising from the same matured promissory note; may both actions proceed?

Answer: No. A party may not divide one cause of action and institute several suits for its component remedies.

Legal Basis: Rule 2, Sections 3 and 4 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Principal and stipulated interest arise from the same breach of the same note and should be claimed in one action; the pendency or judgment in one may bar the other.

Conclusion: The second suit is vulnerable to litis pendentia or res judicata.

All reliefs arising from one cause of action must be asserted in one suit.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • joinder of causes of action
May a plaintiff join a collection claim against one defendant with an unrelated title dispute against a different defendant in one complaint merely because both plaintiffs are the same person?

Answer: No. Joinder is permissive only if the party-joinder rules are observed and, when claims involve different venues or jurisdictions, the joinder satisfies the limits in Rule 2.

Legal Basis: Rule 2, Sections 5 and 6, in relation to Rule 3, Section 6 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The unrelated claims do not arise from the same transaction or series and present no common controlling question sufficient to join the defendants.

Conclusion: The claims should be severed or separately filed in the proper courts.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • real party in interest
A shareholder sues in his own name to collect a debt concededly owed to the corporation without alleging a derivative action; is he the proper plaintiff?

Answer: No. The corporation, which owns the claim and stands to benefit from the judgment, is the real party in interest.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Sections 1 and 2 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The shareholder's economic interest in the corporation does not transfer the corporation's separate chose in action to him.

Conclusion: The complaint should be prosecuted by the corporation or satisfy the requirements of a proper derivative suit.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • indispensable parties

In an action seeking cancellation of a deed signed by both co-owners, the plaintiff impleads only one co-owner although the judgment would necessarily determine the other's title; may the court validly decide the merits without the omitted co-owner?

Answer: No. A person whose interest will necessarily be affected and without whom no final determination can be had is indispensable and must be joined.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Sections 7 and 11 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Cancellation would directly extinguish the omitted co-owner's asserted title, so adjudication in that person's absence would deny due process and leave the controversy incomplete.

Conclusion: The court must order joinder before deciding the merits.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • misjoinder and nonjoinder of parties
Should a complaint be dismissed solely because a dispensable party was mistakenly joined?

Answer: No. Misjoinder or nonjoinder of parties is not by itself a ground for dismissal.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Section 11 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The court may drop the dispensable party or add a necessary party on just terms at any stage, while preserving the viable claim.

Conclusion: The proper response is correction of the parties, not automatic dismissal.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Quiz • class suits
Residents sue on behalf of thousands of subdivision buyers over identical unlawful water charges, but the proposed representatives have claims antagonistic to most buyers; is a class suit proper?

Answer: No. A class suit requires a sufficiently numerous class with a common or general interest and representatives who fairly and adequately protect that interest.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Section 12 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Numerosity and a common issue exist, but antagonistic representatives cannot adequately protect the absent buyers.

Conclusion: Class treatment should be denied unless adequate representatives are substituted.

Ten passengers injured in the same bus collision assert separate damages against the operator and driver; may they join as plaintiffs in one action?

An owner residing in Manila seeks recovery of possession and title to land wholly situated in Baguio; where is venue?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • venue of personal actions
A Cebu resident sues a Davao resident for collection of an unsecured loan; absent an exclusive venue agreement, where may the action be filed?

Answer: At the plaintiff's election, the personal action may be filed where a principal plaintiff resides or where a principal defendant resides.

Legal Basis: Rule 4, Section 2 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Both Cebu and Davao satisfy the general venue rule, assuming the chosen court has subject-matter jurisdiction.

Conclusion: The plaintiff may choose Cebu or Davao.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • exclusive venue agreements
A contract states that litigation 'may be filed in Makati' but contains no words excluding the venues fixed by Rule 4; is Makati the exclusive venue?

Answer: No. Without restrictive language, the stipulation provides an additional permissible venue rather than an exclusive one.

Legal Basis: Rule 4, Section 4(b) of the Rules of Court. A written venue stipulation is exclusive only when restrictive words show that intent; moreover, one who squarely attacks the instrument as forged is not bound at the threshold by the venue clause in that very instrument.

Application: The word 'may' does not waive the ordinary venues and does not say 'exclusively,' 'shall only,' or their equivalent.

Conclusion: A suit in another venue allowed by Rule 4 is not improper on that ground.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • venue clause in an attacked instrument

A homeowner files an action alleging that her signature on a mortgage was forged, while the mortgage says actions 'shall only' be filed in Makati; must her nullity suit be dismissed when filed in her otherwise proper home venue?

Answer: No, not at the threshold solely on the challenged clause. A plaintiff directly denying execution of the instrument cannot logically be bound by a term whose very contractual existence she disputes.

Legal Basis: Rule 4, Sections 1 to 4 of the Rules of Court. A written venue stipulation is exclusive only when restrictive words show that intent; moreover, one who squarely attacks the instrument as forged is not bound at the threshold by the venue clause in that very instrument.

Application: The complaint squarely alleges forgery rather than breach of an admitted mortgage; the ordinary venue rule governs until validity is adjudicated.

Conclusion: The venue-based dismissal should be denied.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • venue against a nonresident defendant
A Philippine resident seeks to exclude a nonresident defendant from an asserted interest in land in Palawan, and the defendant cannot be found in the Philippines; where may the action be commenced?

Answer: It may be commenced where the plaintiff resides or where the property or any portion is situated or found.

Legal Basis: Rule 4, Section 3 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The defendant is a nonresident not found here and the quasi-in-rem action concerns Philippine property.

Conclusion: Either the plaintiff's residence or Palawan is a proper venue, subject to jurisdiction and valid service.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • ultimate facts in pleadings
A complaint merely alleges that 'the defendant is legally liable' without stating the transaction, duty, breach, or resulting injury; is the allegation sufficient?

Answer: No. A pleading must state the ultimate facts supporting the claim, not a bare legal conclusion.

Legal Basis: Rule 8, Section 1 of the Rules of Court. A cause of action is the act or omission violating another's right; failure to state one is tested from the complaint's allegations, hypothetically admitted, together with controlling law of which the court may take notice.

Application: The allegation gives the defendant no factual notice of what conduct created liability and supplies no basis for a responsive admission or denial.

Conclusion: The complaint fails to state a cause of action unless properly amended.
