Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • verification of pleadings
What is the function of verification, and does a defective verification invariably deprive the court of jurisdiction?

Answer: Verification assures that allegations are made in good faith and are true from personal knowledge or authentic records; a defect is generally formal rather than jurisdictional, though the court may require correction.

Legal Basis: Rule 7, Sections 4 and 5 of the Rules of Court. Verification is generally a formal, not jurisdictional, requirement, while certification against forum shopping is mandatory but may be relaxed only for substantial compliance or compelling reasons consistent with the governing rules.

Application: If an authorized affiant substantially knows the material facts and the defect causes no prejudice, correction rather than dismissal may serve justice.

Conclusion: Defective verification does not invariably nullify the action.
Rule 7, Sections 4 and 5 of the Rules of Court. G.R. No. 180986, December 10, 2008, Brion, J. — petition granted; challenged resolutions set aside
Verification is ordinarily a formal requirement susceptible to substantial compliance or timely correction for compelling reasons.
Altres, et al. v. Empleo, et al.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • certification against forum shopping
A corporation's initiatory complaint is accompanied by a certification signed only by outside counsel who shows no special authority or personal knowledge; is that ordinarily sufficient?

Answer: No. The party, or a specifically authorized representative with the required knowledge, must execute the certification; counsel's bare signature is ordinarily insufficient.

Legal Basis: Rule 7, Section 5 of the Rules of Court. Verification is generally a formal, not jurisdictional, requirement, while certification against forum shopping is mandatory but may be relaxed only for substantial compliance or compelling reasons consistent with the governing rules.

Application: Outside counsel has neither shown corporate authorization nor demonstrated personal knowledge of other proceedings.

Conclusion: The complaint is subject to the consequence prescribed by Rule 7 unless a recognized substantial-compliance exception is established.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • electronic filing and service

In a civil case before a first-level court, counsel emails a complaint only to opposing counsel and does not submit the original to the court personally, by registered mail, or by accredited courier; has the action commenced?

Answer: No. Service on an adverse party is distinct from filing with the court. Under current Rule 13-A, an initiatory pleading must first be filed with the court personally, by registered mail, or by accredited courier, and the filing party must then email the digital copy to the court within 24 hours; otherwise it is deemed not filed.

Legal Basis: Rule 1, Section 5 and Rule 13-A, Sections 2 and 3 of the Rules of Court, as amended by A.M. No. 19-10-20-SC (November 26, 2024; effective December 1, 2024). The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Counsel merely served an email on the opposing side and completed neither the prescribed primary filing with the court nor the required electronic transmittal to the court.

Conclusion: The complaint is deemed not filed and the action has not commenced.

Rule 1, Section 5 and Rule 13-A, Sections 2 and 3 of the Rules of Court, as amended by A.M. No. 19-10-20-SC (November 26, 2024; effective December 1, 2024). A.M. No. 19-10-20-SC, October 15, 2019, En Banc Resolution — 2019 Amendments effective May 1, 2020; further amended by Rule 13-A, November 26, 2024, effective December 1, 2024
For covered civil cases, filing and service are distinct; an initiatory pleading requires both a prescribed primary filing with the court and timely electronic transmittal to the court.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • actionable documents
A defendant admits signing the attached promissory note but alleges payment; must she deny the note's genuineness and due execution under oath to preserve payment as a defense?

Answer: No. The special sworn denial concerns genuineness and due execution; payment is a separate affirmative defense that may be pleaded even while execution is admitted.

Legal Basis: Rule 8, Sections 7 and 8 of the Rules of Court. Failure to deny under oath the genuineness and due execution of an actionable document results in an admission that permits the document to be considered without further authentication, subject to defenses not covered by that admission.

Application: By admitting the signature, the defendant removes authentication from dispute but may still prove that the admitted obligation was extinguished.

Conclusion: The payment defense is not waived merely because no sworn denial of execution was made.

Admission of an actionable document's genuineness and due execution does not admit independent defenses such as payment, prescription, or illegality.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • specific denials
A defendant answers every material paragraph with 'defendant has no knowledge sufficient to form a belief' despite personally participating in the transaction; is this an effective specific denial?

Answer: No. A denial for lack of knowledge must be made in good faith; when the matter is plainly within the defendant's knowledge, the evasive denial may be treated as an admission.

Legal Basis: Rule 8, Sections 10 and 11 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The defendant personally negotiated the transaction and cannot credibly profess total ignorance of its material events.

Conclusion: The material allegations may be deemed admitted.

After May 1, 2020, a defendant files a prohibited omnibus motion to dismiss based only on failure to state a cause of action; what is the proper procedural treatment?

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • compulsory counterclaims

A seller sues for the unpaid price, and the buyer has a matured damages claim arising from defects in the same goods; what happens if the buyer omits that claim from the answer without leave to amend?

Answer: The damages claim is compulsory because it arises from the same transaction and ordinarily is barred if not pleaded.

Legal Basis: Rule 6, Sections 6 and 7; Rule 11, Section 10 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The price and defect claims concern the same sale, parties, and evidence, and no third party beyond the court's jurisdiction is indispensable to the counterclaim.

Conclusion: The buyer should plead it in the action or timely obtain leave to set up the omitted counterclaim.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • cross-claims
Distinguish a cross-claim from a counterclaim using a collision suit against a driver and vehicle owner?

Answer: A counterclaim is asserted against an opposing party, while a cross-claim is asserted against a co-party and must arise from the transaction or occurrence involved in the original action or a counterclaim.

Legal Basis: Rule 6, Sections 6 and 8 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The owner's indemnity claim against the co-defendant driver arising from the same collision is a cross-claim, not a counterclaim against the plaintiff.

Conclusion: The owner should plead the indemnity demand as a cross-claim.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • third-party complaints
A contractor sued for defective work seeks leave to implead its insurer solely for indemnity under a policy covering the same loss; is a third-party complaint conceptually proper?

Answer: Yes, if the proposed claim is for contribution, indemnity, subrogation, or other relief in respect of the plaintiff's claim and will not inject a wholly separate controversy.

Legal Basis: Rule 6, Section 11 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The insurer's alleged duty is derivative of the contractor's potential liability for the same defective work.

Conclusion: The court may admit the third-party complaint on just terms.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • limited function of a reply
The answer alleges payment but attaches no actionable document; must the plaintiff file a reply to avoid admitting payment?

Answer: No. New matters in the answer are deemed controverted, and a reply is allowed only in the limited situation involving an actionable document attached to the answer.

Legal Basis: Rule 6, Section 10 of the Rules of Court, as amended. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Because no actionable document is attached, payment is automatically controverted and the plaintiff need not reply.

Conclusion: Failure to file a reply does not admit payment.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • amendment as a matter of right
May a plaintiff amend the complaint once without leave after a motion attacking it has been served but before any answer is served?

Answer: Yes. A party may amend once as a matter of right before a responsive pleading is served; a motion is not a responsive pleading.

Legal Basis: Rule 10, Section 2 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: No answer has been served, and the plaintiff has not previously used the one amendment as of right.

Conclusion: The amendment may be filed without leave.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • amendment by leave and jurisdiction
A complaint states no cause of action and is filed in a court lacking subject-matter jurisdiction; may amendment by leave be used solely to manufacture jurisdiction retroactively?

Answer: No. Leave shall be refused when amendment is intended to confer jurisdiction or when the original pleading stated no cause of action from the beginning that could be amended under the rule.

Legal Basis: Rule 10, Section 3 of the Rules of Court, as amended. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Jurisdiction is determined by law and the original allegations; a party cannot create it retroactively by substantial amendment.

Conclusion: The court should deny leave and dismiss without prejudice to a proper action where appropriate.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • relation back of amendments
After prescription runs, a plaintiff corrects a misdescription of the same transaction and injury already fully alleged in the timely original complaint; does the correction necessarily prescribe?

Answer: No. An amendment may relate back when the claim or defense in it arose from the conduct, transaction, or occurrence set forth or attempted to be set forth in the original pleading.

Legal Basis: Rule 10, Section 5 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The defendant had timely notice of the operative event and injury; the amendment changes description rather than introducing a new cause based on different facts.

Conclusion: The correction relates back, absent prejudice or a genuinely new cause of action.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Midterm • supplemental pleadings
A creditor files suit before the debt matures and, after maturity, asks to supplement the complaint with the later default; may the supplemental pleading cure the premature action?

Answer: No. A supplemental pleading may allege later events but cannot create a cause of action that did not exist when the original complaint was filed.

Legal Basis: Rule 10, Section 6 of the Rules of Court. A supplemental pleading concerns transactions occurring after the original pleading but cannot cure the absence of a cause of action when the original complaint was filed; an amendment may conform pleadings to issues actually tried by consent.

Application: At commencement there was no enforceable default; later maturity cannot retroactively supply the missing original cause.

Conclusion: The premature complaint should be dismissed without prejudice to a new timely action.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • personal and substituted service of summons
A sheriff makes one unproductive visit, leaves summons with a neighboring shopkeeper, and gives no reason why personal service was impracticable; is service valid?

Answer: No. Substituted service is permitted only after personal service cannot be promptly made for justifiable causes, and the return must state the efforts and circumstances warranting substitution.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Sections 6 and 7 of the Rules of Court, as amended. Valid service of summons or voluntary appearance is indispensable to jurisdiction over the defendant; substituted service requires diligent prior attempts and a return stating the material circumstances with particularity.

Application: One unexplained attempt and delivery to a neighbor outside the defendant's residence or office do not meet the rule.

Conclusion: The court has not acquired jurisdiction over the defendant through that service.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • substituted service through electronic means
After repeated documented attempts at personal service, may a court authorize summons through the defendant's verified email or social-media account?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • summons on private juridical entities

A summons for a domestic corporation is served at its principal office on the employee who customarily receives its correspondence after the enumerated officers are unavailable; is service permitted under the current rule?

Answer: Yes. The current Rule permits service on the customary correspondence recipient at the principal office when service cannot be made on the enumerated officers or their secretaries.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Section 12 of the Rules of Court, as amended. Conclusion: Service is valid under the liberalized current rule.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • summons on public corporations
Summons against a chartered government-owned corporation is delivered only to a field-office legal assistant, not its executive head or another officer directed by law or the court; is service valid?

Answer: No. A chartered public corporation is served through its executive head or another officer authorized by law or directed by the court.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Section 15 of the Rules of Court, as applied in Beltran. The 2019 Rules liberalized service on private juridical entities, retained a distinct rule for public corporations, and introduced deputation of counsel who specially appears to contest defective service so the case can proceed after proper service.

Application: A field legal assistant is not the executive head, and neither law nor a court order designated that employee to receive summons.

Conclusion: The initial service is defective, although the court may employ the remedial mechanism in Rule 14, Section 13.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • deputation of counsel to serve summons
Counsel specially appears solely to challenge defective summons on a defendant; under the current Rules, must the case be dismissed immediately?

Answer: No. The court shall deputize that counsel to serve summons on the client, curing the service problem while preserving the special appearance.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Section 13 of the Rules of Court, as amended. The 2019 Rules liberalized service on private juridical entities, retained a distinct rule for public corporations, and introduced deputation of counsel who specially appears to contest defective service so the case can proceed after proper service.

Application: Counsel already has contact with and authority from the defendant and can perform the court-imposed service duty without treating the jurisdictional objection as waived.

Conclusion: The court should direct counsel to serve the summons rather than automatically dismiss.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • extraterritorial service
May extraterritorial service alone support a Philippine money judgment in a purely in-personam collection suit against a nonresident who owns no attached property here and never appears?

Answer: No. Extraterritorial service under Rule 14 operates in actions involving status or property within the Philippines, not to create personal jurisdiction for a purely in-personam money claim.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Sections 16 and 17 of the Rules of Court, as amended. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The suit concerns only personal liability, no local res is before the court, and the nonresident has not submitted to jurisdiction.

Conclusion: A personal money judgment cannot rest on publication or overseas notice alone.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • voluntary appearance
A defendant who was not validly served files a motion asking the court to dismiss on the merits without expressly objecting to personal jurisdiction; has she submitted to the court?

Answer: Yes. Seeking affirmative relief without an explicit jurisdictional objection constitutes voluntary appearance equivalent to service of summons.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Section 23 of the Rules of Court, as amended. Valid service of summons or voluntary appearance is indispensable to jurisdiction over the defendant; substituted service requires diligent prior attempts and a return stating the material circumstances with particularity.

Application: The defendant invoked adjudication on the merits and did not preserve a special appearance challenging jurisdiction over her person.

Conclusion: The court acquired personal jurisdiction through voluntary appearance.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • period to answer and extension
A defendant receives summons and seeks two successive thirty-day extensions to answer based only on workload; may both be granted?

Answer: No. An answer is due within the period fixed by Rule 11, and only one extension of not more than thirty calendar days may be granted for meritorious reasons.

Legal Basis: Rule 11, Sections 1 and 11 of the Rules of Court, as amended. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Ordinary workload is not automatically meritorious, and the second extension is prohibited.

Conclusion: At most one justified extension may be allowed.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • declaration of default
May a court declare a defendant in default on its own initiative immediately after the answer period expires?

Answer: No. The claiming party must file a motion with notice and prove the defending party's failure to answer within the allowed time.

Legal Basis: Rule 9, Section 3 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Without a noticed motion and proof of default, the adverse consequence cannot validly be imposed sua sponte.

Conclusion: A spontaneous default order is improper.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • relief from order of default
Before judgment, a defendant moves to lift an order of default and shows that a hospital confinement caused the delay and that receipts establish full payment; should relief be considered?

Answer: Yes. Before judgment, default may be set aside upon a showing of fraud, accident, mistake, or excusable negligence and a meritorious defense.

Legal Basis: Rule 9, Section 3(b) of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Documented confinement may constitute excusable negligence, and the payment receipts disclose a concrete defense rather than a bare conclusion.

Conclusion: The court should set aside default on just terms if the showing is credible.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • mandatory pre-trial submissions
Counsel appears at pre-trial but files no pre-trial brief and offers no lawful excuse; what is the consequence for the plaintiff?

Answer: Failure to file the required pre-trial brief has the same effect as failure to appear and may lead to dismissal of the plaintiff's action, subject to the court's evaluation of a valid excuse and due process.

Legal Basis: Rule 18, Sections 5 and 6 of the Rules of Court, as amended. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: Mere physical appearance does not cure the omitted brief, which is essential to admissions, stipulations, witnesses, and exhibits.

Conclusion: The court may impose the Rule 18 consequence after hearing any proffered excuse.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • depositions pending action
A party notices the deposition of an adverse witness for discovery, and the witness objects that depositions may be taken only when the witness will be unavailable at trial; is the objection correct?

Answer: No. Depositions may be used to discover information and preserve testimony; unavailability limits some uses at trial but is not a prerequisite to taking the deposition.

Legal Basis: Rule 23, Sections 1, 2, and 4 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The proposed questioning seeks nonprivileged matter relevant to the claims and defenses, so the deposition may proceed subject to protective orders.

Conclusion: The deposition is permissible despite no present showing of trial unavailability.

A plaintiff never serves written interrogatories on the defendant and later seeks to call that defendant as an adverse witness without leave; may the court refuse?

Answer: Yes. A party who unjustifiably fails to serve written interrogatories may not compel the adverse party to testify in open court or by deposition without leave on good cause shown.

Application: The plaintiff bypassed the discovery mechanism and offers no good cause for doing so.

Conclusion: The court may deny the attempt to compel adverse testimony.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • requests for admission
A party served with a proper request for admission files no sworn response within the period fixed by the Rule; what is the effect?

Answer: Each properly requested matter is deemed admitted for the pending action, unless the court later permits withdrawal or amendment to serve the merits without prejudice.

Legal Basis: Rule 26, Sections 2 to 4 of the Rules of Court. Matters properly requested are deemed admitted when the served party fails to make a timely sworn denial; the resulting admissions may establish the absence of a genuine factual issue and support summary judgment.

Application: The unanswered requests establish the genuineness and transaction facts and may remove any genuine factual issue.

Conclusion: The admissions bind the served party in this case unless validly withdrawn.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • production and trade-secret privilege
A distributor demands its opponent's entire secret manufacturing formula although sales records can establish the amount in dispute; must production be compelled?

Answer: Not automatically. Discovery reaches relevant nonprivileged matter, but the court must protect trade secrets and may deny or narrowly tailor production when the need is not shown to outweigh the harm.

Legal Basis: Rule 27, Section 1 and Rule 23, Section 16 of the Rules of Court. Discovery is broad but not unlimited; a court may deny production of information protected by a recognized privilege, including trade secrets, when the requesting party fails to overcome the protection.

Application: The formula is commercially sensitive and cumulative because sales records can prove the disputed amount.

Conclusion: The court should deny the overbroad demand or impose a tightly limited protective order.

Civil Procedure I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 2 • JD602 • Final • physical or mental examination
In a damages suit where the plaintiff alleges permanent neurological injury, may the defendant obtain a court-ordered medical examination merely by notice?

Answer: No. Because the condition is in controversy, the court may order an examination only on motion for good cause, notice, and an order specifying the examiner, scope, time, place, manner, and conditions.

Legal Basis: Rule 28, Section 1 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court approved the amended Rules to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive disposition of actions; Rule 13-A now governs mandatory electronic filing and service in covered first- and second-level civil cases.

Application: The alleged neurological injury satisfies the in-controversy element, but a judicial order on a supported motion remains necessary.

Conclusion: The examination may be ordered only after the Rule 28 safeguards are met.

Compulsory physical or mental examination requires condition in controversy, good cause, notice, and a specific court order.
